title: C++ Standards Timeline and Where to Go Next
summary: C++ gets a new standard every three years. Knowing what arrived when helps you read older code, choose compiler settings and know what you can rely on. After that: pick a field and go deep.
markdown:
## What each standard added ```mermaid flowchart LR A["C++98 / 03
templates, the STL,
exceptions"] --> B["C++11
auto, lambdas, move,
smart pointers, threads,
constexpr, range-for"] B --> C["C++14
generic lambdas,
make_unique"] C --> D["C++17
optional, variant,
string_view, filesystem,
structured bindings,
if constexpr"] D --> E["C++20
concepts, ranges,
coroutines, modules,
format, span"] E --> F["C++23
print, expected,
generator,
import std"] F --> G["C++26
reflection,
contracts,
std::execution"] ``` | Standard | Principal additions | In this course | |---|---|---| | **C++98 / 03** | Classes, templates, exceptions, the containers and algorithms | The foundation of everything | | **C++11** | `auto`, lambdas, rvalue references and move semantics, `unique_ptr` and `shared_ptr`, threads and atomics, `constexpr`, range-based `for`, `nullptr`, `enum class`, variadic templates, `override` | Milestones 4 to 12 | | **C++14** | Generic lambdas, `std::make_unique`, `decltype(auto)`, binary literals, digit separators | Milestones 2 and 5 | | **C++17** | `optional`, `variant`, `any`, `string_view`, `filesystem`, structured bindings, `if constexpr`, fold expressions, CTAD, inline variables, parallel algorithms, guaranteed copy elision | Milestones 9 to 12 | | **C++20** | Concepts, ranges, coroutines, modules, `<=>`, `std::format`, `span`, `jthread`, semaphores and latches, `consteval` and `constinit`, designated initializers, calendars and time zones | Milestones 9 to 13 | | **C++23** | `std::print`, `std::expected`, `std::generator`, `mdspan`, `flat_map`, `import std`, deducing `this`, `ranges::to`, `views::zip` and `enumerate` | Milestones 10 to 13 | | **C++26** | Static reflection, contracts, `std::execution`, `#embed`, linear algebra, defined behaviour for uninitialized reads | Mentioned in Milestones 11 to 13 | C++11 was the turning point. Code written before it looks like a different language, with raw `new` and `delete`, hand-written iterator loops and no `auto`. "Modern C++" means C++11 and later. > [!note] A standard and its implementation are different things > A feature is usable only once your compiler **and** its standard library implement it, which can lag the standard by years. cppreference.com keeps a compiler-support table for each feature. ## Reading older code You will spend more time reading existing code than writing new code. A translation table: | In older code | Today | |---|---| | `new` and `delete` | `std::make_unique`, containers | | `NULL` or `0` for a pointer | `nullptr` | | `typedef` | `using` | | `for (iterator it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ++it)` | A range-based `for` | | A hand-written function object class | A lambda | | `std::enable_if` | A concept | | Output parameters for several results | Return a struct, or structured bindings | | `printf`, or chains of `<<` with manipulators | `std::format`, `std::print` | | A `char*` and a length | `std::string_view`, `std::span` | ## Where to go next You have covered the language. Depth now comes from a field. ```mermaid mindmap root((Your path)) Games raylib, SFML, SDL OpenGL, Vulkan, DirectX Unreal Engine Entity component systems Systems Operating system internals Networking with Asio Embedded devices Compilers and LLVM Performance SIMD GPU computing High-performance computing Finance Low-latency systems Lock-free structures Tools and applications Qt Dear ImGui Command-line tools Open source Contribute to a library Read the standard library ``` Since your aim is computer science, three subjects build directly on this course and are worth taking next: **data structures and algorithms** (trees, graphs, hashing, dynamic programming), **computer architecture** (what [[13.04 Performance, Caches and Data-Oriented Design]] only sketched), and **operating systems** (what threads, memory and files really are). C++ is the language most of that material is taught and implemented in. ### Resources | Kind | Recommendation | |---|---| | Reference | **cppreference.com**. Keep it open. | | Guidelines | The **C++ Core Guidelines** | | Books: foundations | *A Tour of C++* and *Programming: Principles and Practice Using C++*, both by Stroustrup | | Books: using it well | *Effective Modern C++* (Meyers); *C++ Concurrency in Action* (Williams); *C++ Templates: The Complete Guide* (Vandevoorde, Josuttis, Gregor) | | Books: performance | *Optimized C++* (Guntheroth); *Data-Oriented Design* (Fabian) | | Talks | CppCon, C++Now and Meeting C++, all online. Start with the "Back to Basics" series. | | Experiment | **Compiler Explorer** (godbolt.org) shows the machine code. **C++ Insights** shows what the compiler makes of your source. | | Practice | Advent of Code, Exercism's C++ track, contributing to open source | ## Four pieces of advice | | | |---|---| | **Build things** | Every project you finish teaches more than any lesson. The projects in this course are a start; the ones you invent yourself teach the most. | | **Read other people's code** | Good libraries, and the standard library's own implementation, show how experienced programmers solve problems. | | **Keep the safety net on** | Warnings, sanitizers and tests, always: [[13.09 Testing, Sanitizers, Static Analysis and Tooling]] | | **Simple first, clever later** | The best C++ is unremarkable to read. Reach for the advanced techniques of the last three milestones when a problem needs them, and not before. |

cards.q: Which standard is the start of "modern C++"?
cards.a: C++11, which added `auto`, lambdas, move semantics, smart pointers and much else.

cards.q: Why might a feature in the current standard be unavailable to you?
cards.a: A feature can be used only when both your compiler and its standard library have implemented it.

How often is a new C++ standard published?
